text: The most important function of a university is to create an atmosphere in which creative thinking can flourish. It is not enough to transmit knowledge from one generation to the next. A university must be a place where knowledge is created, where the boundaries of human understanding are pushed outward. This requires an environment of intellectual freedom, rigorous inquiry, and tolerance for unconventional ideas. The greatest universities in the world are those that have fostered this atmosphere, and it is this atmosphere that we must create in India.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, Address at IIM Ahmedabad Convocation, 1966

text: Education in India faces a paradox of enormous proportions. We have some of the finest minds in the world, yet the vast majority of our population has no access to quality education. The traditional model of building more schools and training more teachers, while essential, is simply too slow to address the scale of the problem. We need a radical new approach, and I believe that technology — specifically satellite television — holds the key. Imagine a single brilliant teacher conducting a lesson that reaches not thirty students, but thirty million. This is not science fiction. The technology exists today. What we need is the imagination and the will to deploy it.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, Lecture on Technology and Education, 1969

text: The founding of the Indian Institute of Management in Ahmedabad was driven by a conviction that India's scientific and industrial progress requires world-class management education. It is not enough to have brilliant scientists and engineers if we lack the organizational capability to translate their innovations into practical outcomes. Management is not merely administration — it is the science of getting things done efficiently, ethically, and at scale. IIM Ahmedabad must produce leaders who can build and run institutions that serve the national interest.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, IIM Ahmedabad Foundation Document, 1962

text: The Community Science Centre that we have established in Ahmedabad serves a purpose that I consider absolutely fundamental to India's future. We must cultivate a scientific temper among our people — not just among university graduates, but among children, farmers, artisans, and ordinary citizens. The scientific temper is not about memorising formulas or understanding complex theories. It is about developing the habit of asking why, of demanding evidence, of testing assumptions against reality. A nation that thinks scientifically is a nation that can solve its own problems.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, Inauguration of Community Science Centre, 1966

text: Rural education in India cannot wait for the slow accumulation of physical infrastructure. We need to find ways to bring quality education to hundreds of thousands of villages simultaneously. The Satellite Instructional Television Experiment is designed to test whether satellite broadcasting can be an effective medium for this purpose. We will broadcast programmes on agriculture, health, family planning, and basic science directly to community viewing centres in rural areas. If this experiment succeeds — and I am convinced it will — it will revolutionise our approach to education and rural development.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, SITE Planning Committee Address, 1970

text: Science education must begin with wonder. A child who looks at the night sky and asks why the stars shine is already a scientist. Our task as educators is not to extinguish that wonder with rote learning and examinations, but to nurture it, to guide it, to show the child that the same spirit of inquiry that drove Galileo and Newton and Raman is alive in them. The Community Science Centre in Ahmedabad is built on this philosophy. Every exhibit, every demonstration, every programme is designed to provoke curiosity and encourage hands-on exploration.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, Essay on Science Education, 1967

text: I believe that the creation of institutions is perhaps the most important contribution that any individual can make to a society. Institutions outlive individuals. They create ecosystems in which talent can flourish across generations. When I established PRL, I did not merely create a laboratory — I created a culture of scientific inquiry that would attract and nurture the best minds in physics for decades to come. The same principle guided the establishment of ATIRA, IIM Ahmedabad, and ISRO. Each of these institutions is designed to be self-sustaining, to evolve with the times, and to continue serving the nation long after its founders are gone.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, Reflections on Institution Building, 1970

text: The strength of an institution lies not in its buildings or its budget, but in its people and its culture. At PRL, we have always believed in giving young researchers extraordinary freedom and responsibility. A twenty-five-year-old scientist at PRL may lead a research team, design experiments, and publish papers in international journals. This trust in youth is not reckless — it is strategic. Young minds are unencumbered by convention, willing to take risks, and driven by a passion that older, more established scientists sometimes lose. By empowering them early, we accelerate the pace of discovery and build a culture of excellence.

The relationship between science and the arts is not one of opposition but of deep complementarity. My wife Mrinalini and I founded the Darpana Academy of Performing Arts because we believe that a complete human being — and a complete society — requires both scientific understanding and artistic expression. The scientist and the artist both seek truth, both require discipline and creativity, and both expand the boundaries of human experience. A nation that cultivates only its scientific talent while neglecting its artistic heritage is a nation that is impoverished in spirit.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, Darpana Academy Anniversary Speech, 1964

text: Technology transfer is not simply about acquiring machines or technical drawings from abroad. True technology transfer requires building indigenous capability — the ability to understand, modify, improve, and eventually surpass the imported technology. This is why every international collaboration that we enter into must include a strong training component. Our scientists and engineers must not merely operate foreign equipment; they must understand its principles well enough to design their own. Self-reliance in technology is not about isolation from the world. It is about engaging with the world from a position of knowledge and strength.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, Address on Technology Policy, 1968
